title: Nvidia plunges 14% as an SEC accounting report caps its longest weekly losing streak since 2008
summary: Nvidia shares tumbled 14% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day and closing lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008, CNBC reported on November 20, 2026. Reuters reported Friday that the Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring potential accounting issues at Nvidia, pushing the stock down further. Over the seven weeks the shares are down 46%, erasing about $2.6 trillion in market value; once the world’s most valuable company, Nvidia is now worth $3 trillion, fourth behind Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet, and trades at roughly 8.4 times forward earnings versus 29 times for AMD. The company is reeling from the removal of co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12 after multiple reported affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy. Even a better-than-expected earnings report didn’t stem the selling, though interim CEO Colette Kress projected 75% revenue growth next fiscal year and signed off Tuesday’s call by saying, “we’ve got this.”

title: California’s attorney general subpoenas Nvidia over Huang’s alleged China ties
summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta said Thursday evening that the state has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy, TechCrunch reported on November 20, 2026. The state wants to find out whether Nvidia’s advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and whether the company misled investors and the public. “The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said. “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” he wrote. Nvidia’s board has hired a law firm and an independent slate of directors to investigate, the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company’s disclosures, and Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

title: Trump vows to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad, threatening a ‘tremendous tax’
summary: President Donald Trump said Friday that U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers in other countries and will face a “tremendous tax” penalty if they do, CNBC reported on November 20, 2026. “We’re going to fight very hard for the data centers,” Trump said at a White House press conference, in a policy announcement that apparently came as news to his own staff. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now they’re here.” If companies want to keep building centers outside the U.S., “they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them,” he added. The push comes even though CNBC’s All-America Economic Survey found 64% of registered voters opposed an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, with just 13% in support. Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle have already built data centers in other countries; Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Oracle did not immediately respond to CNBC.

title: Signal blocks screenshots so AI agents like Gemini and Siri can’t read your chats
summary: Signal is restricting screenshots on Android and iOS in an effort to keep AI agents from reading users’ messages, The Verge reported on November 20, 2026. Agentic AI built into operating systems that analyzes on-screen information is “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post. Blocking screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android should prevent Siri, Gemini and other Android assistants from reading on-screen content; users can turn screenshots back on in settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Signal took a similar approach last year against Microsoft’s Recall feature, and is now calling on Apple, Google and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to developers. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights,” Whittaker said.

title: Cursor tells lawmakers it may phase out Chinese AI models over ‘geopolitical risk’
summary: SpaceX’s AI coding platform Cursor is considering moving away from Chinese AI models because of “geopolitical risk,” CNBC reported on November 20, 2026. Cursor, which SpaceX acquired at an implied $60 billion equity value in August, built its coding model Composer 2 on top of Moonshot AI’s Kimi K2.5. It now plans to “explore phasing out PRC-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk,” according to a report by the House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China, shared with CNBC ahead of its Friday publication. Airbnb and DoorDash also engaged with the months-long investigation. The report found that cost, customization and near-frontier performance were driving adoption of Chinese models, with the U.S. lacking a competitive open-weight alternative at the “price and performance the market demands.” Its recommendations include a “national American open-weight initiative” combining public computing power, shared evaluation infrastructure and “lawful access” to American frontier models for training.

title: S&P 500 and Dow close in correction as the Nasdaq posts its worst week since March 2020
summary: The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average closed Friday in correction territory, more than 10% off their records, CNBC reported on November 20, 2026, while the Nasdaq Composite lost its gain for the year and the Nasdaq-100 briefly entered a bear market intraday. The Nasdaq fell 10% for the week, its worst since the Covid plunge of March 2020. CNBC pointed to Anthropic’s IPO as a possible “sell the news” moment for the AI trade, along with Nvidia’s 14% Friday drop, the S&P 500’s break below its 200-day moving average, inflation pressure on the Federal Reserve and slowing earnings growth. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said the Fed may need a half-point hike next month: “I’m very, very concerned about inflation.” Wharton professor Jeremy Siegel called it a run-of-the-mill correction after the S&P 500 returned more than 20% in 2023 and 2024 and 16% last year. “People began to think that 15 to 20 [percent] was going to be the norm with AI,” he said. “Stay with your stocks.”

title: Anthropic falls 8.5% in its first full day of trading as tech stocks get shellacked
summary: Anthropic shares fell 8.5% on Friday to close their first full day of trading, CNBC reported on November 20, 2026, as worries about the AI trade dragged tech stocks lower. The stock opened at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday after the company raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO of all time, then slid to close that day at $97.17. On Friday, chipmakers Nvidia and AMD both plummeted more than 13%, and Amazon, Google and Microsoft also closed lower. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Anthropic an “only in America story”: “Anthropic in 2021 was seven people sitting around during Covid in a park in San Francisco, with laptops and a dream, and then yesterday we saw the most valuable IPO in history.” Analysts were split. Seaport Research rated the stock neutral, calling it “an incredible leap of faith by investors,” while William Blair rated it outperform, saying it could become “a significantly profitable business over time.”

title: TSMC slides as Taiwan’s Taiex suffers its worst week since 1991
summary: Taiwan’s Taiex fell 6.2% to 36,033.29 on Friday, Nov. 20, capping a 17.5% weekly drop, its worst week since 1991, Chip Dispatch reported. TSMC closed at NT$2,000 in Taipei, down 4.8%, and its U.S.-listed shares ended Thursday at $352.09, down 11.7% for the week. On Thursday, TSMC had narrowly avoided a short-selling price restriction, falling 3.45% to NT$2,100, just 0.05 percentage point below the regulator’s 3.5% trigger, Chip Dispatch noted; the company accounts for more than 40% of Taiwan’s market value. The selloff began on Wall Street Thursday, when the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.3% and AMD sank 7.7% after a short seller’s report, then ran through Asia: South Korea’s KOSPI dropped 5.2% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 5.1%. In Taipei, Delta Electronics fell by the 10% daily limit and MediaTek lost almost 10%. Reuters said MSCI’s Asia-Pacific index outside Japan was down 8.3% for the week, its worst since March 2020.

title: SoftBank suffers its worst day in over two years as the AI sell-off hits Asia
summary: Shares in Japan’s SoftBank Group closed 14.48% lower on Friday, their worst day since August 2024, as a sell-off swept through Asian technology stocks following Anthropic’s market debut, CNBC reported on November 20, 2026. The drop underscores investor worries about SoftBank’s aggressive AI bets, particularly its exposure to OpenAI, Anthropic’s rival, in which it has invested a total of $64.6 billion. SoftBank’s OpenAI stake and its ownership of chip designer Arm have made the shares especially sensitive to swings in AI sentiment; the stock lost 30% in October and is down 31% so far this month. Japanese chip stocks also tumbled, with Tokyo Electron closing 7.06% lower, Lasertec shedding 9.21% and Renesas Electronics losing 7.02%. In South Korea, Nvidia suppliers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics fell 5.92% and 7.01%, dragging the Kospi down 5.21%, and TSMC closed 4.76% lower in Taiwan.

title: Tencent publishes open weights for its full 770-billion-parameter Hy4 flagship
summary: Tencent has published downloadable weights for its full flagship Hy4 model, Open Model Weights reported on November 21, 2026, completing a release it announced on November 4 with weights promised to follow. The official repository now lists three artifacts: instruction-tuned Hy4, an FP8 instruction checkpoint and a pretrained Hy4 base. Tencent describes Hy4 as a multimodal mixture-of-experts model with a 770-billion-parameter language backbone and 49 billion active parameters per token, plus a 1.23-billion-parameter vision transformer and a 3.3-billion-parameter speculative-decoding drafter. It understands text, images and video and advertises a context ceiling of 1,048,576 tokens, with deployment recipes for vLLM and SGLang. The weights ship under Tencent’s own Hy License, not Apache 2.0, Open Model Weights cautioned. Tencent reports strong results on computer use, office workflows and research tasks, while acknowledging gaps against top proprietary systems; Open Model Weights says it has not reproduced those claims.

title: Thinking Machines’ Inkling 2 Mini loops its layers to run coding agents on a laptop
summary: Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weight model built to make coding-agent work feasible on local computers, Open Model Weights reported on November 21, 2026. Published November 20, it is a 26.4-billion-parameter mixture of experts with about 3.4 billion parameters active, shipped in a mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 checkpoint of roughly 20GB; the company recommends 32GB or more of memory. Its novelty is a loop: of 24 physical decoder layers, the twelve middle ones run three times with shared parameters, producing 48 layer applications per token. It accepts text and images, has a published context ceiling of one million tokens, and has day-one recipes for Transformers, llama.cpp, MLX on Apple silicon and SGLang. Thinking Machines reports strong coding-agent, search and tool-use results against similarly sized open models and discloses weaker results on some instruction-following tests. The weights are Apache 2.0 with a separate acceptable-use policy.

title: Microsoft releases Aion, a small MIT-licensed model meant to power future Windows features
summary: Microsoft’s Windows Applied Sciences Group has published Aion 1.0 Instruct, a 2.3-billion-parameter language model for local text tasks, Open Model Weights reported on November 19, 2026. The Hugging Face model card declares an MIT license and lists weights, configuration, tokenizer and code. The model has a 32,768-token context limit and a hybrid attention stack of 21 sliding-window layers and seven full-attention layers, and supports eight languages: English, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, French, Chinese and Japanese. It targets everyday work such as summarizing and rewriting documents, answering questions and understanding email threads. Microsoft says an optimized version, paired with a content-moderation model, is planned to become a Windows small language model by the end of January 2027; that integration has not happened yet. Microsoft self-reports 55.15 on MMLU and 83.90 on its IFEval aggregation. Open Model Weights notes the quickstart requires trust_remote_code, which deserves careful review.

title: AI helped claim a proof of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, and a human posted one too
summary: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge appears to have found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, a problem dating to 1859 and one of the Millennium Prize problems, TechCrunch reported on November 20, 2026. Several mathematicians on the Zulip chat, including MIT’s Andrew Sutherland, said they confirmed that the formal proof compiles, though it will take a while for the community to understand it. Alpöge described working through the argument “through incredible confusion with Claude,” and wrote that the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line”; he has committed to producing a human-intelligible explanation. Meanwhile, Stanford professor Ravi Vakil posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting “it is all human, with no AI.” Masullo, who said it is the result of 12 years of work, wrote to discouraged mathematicians: “we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”

title: Super-hot rock geothermal heats up as Google signs a $500 million-plus deal with Quaise
summary: Geothermal startups are racing to tap the deepest, hottest rocks, and the winners could power the grid and AI data centers, TechCrunch reported on November 20, 2026. At extreme depths water turns into a supercritical fluid that carries tremendous energy, and a single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts or more. Quaise Energy said Tuesday that Google will pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts from a Quaise project in central Oregon that will tap heat three miles deep. Starting about 2.5 miles down, Quaise swaps its drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron that bombards rock with millimeter-wave radiation, turning it to ash. Rival Mazama Energy announced Carbon Chill, which uses carbon dioxide instead of drilling mud to keep conventional bits cool. Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and the CO2 cooling cut drilling time another 20%, CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch. The U.S. has up to 57 terawatts of geothermal potential.

title: Daniel Ek backs Europa Fusion, an AI researcher’s simulation-first fusion startup
summary: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy U.K. fusion power startup founded by AI researcher Nantas Nardelli, TechCrunch reported in an exclusive on November 20, 2026, after Bloomberg first reported the investment. Founded in February, the startup is led by Nardelli, who previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research and Microsoft Research Cambridge and was recently head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion. Where most fusion startups lean heavily on physical test devices, Nardelli believes fusion companies should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source told TechCrunch. Like Pacific Fusion, Europa will pursue pulsed power, using massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until atoms fuse. No one has yet built a fusion plant that supplies electricity to the grid, but the technology could ease worries about AI’s energy use. “I used to build robots for a living,” Nardelli wrote. “One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”

title: A Kansas community raises $37,000 to replace a teen landscaper’s stolen equipment
summary: When thieves took about $20,000 in machinery from a Kansas teen’s landscaping business, his community raised money to replace all of it, Good News Network reported on November 20, 2026. Sonny Gallardo of Prairie Village started the business in 6th grade, going door to door raking leaves after school with supplies his grandpa dropped off. Four years later, Gallardo’s Sunnyside Jobs LLC had enough equipment for a 5-person crew, until someone came in the night before Halloween and unhooked his 10-foot trailer with all 5 lawnmowers. He was still working on insurance and coverage wasn’t yet in place. A GoFundMe organized on his behalf raised $37,000. “The world would be a much better place with more ppl like you in it, and we are cheering you on young man; we see you and we’ve got your back,” wrote a pair of donors, who encouraged him to get the best equipment he could.

title: Every Tuesday, a Toronto chef cooks lunch for 100 people from random food bank ingredients
summary: Every Tuesday for years, Toronto-area chef Maddy Goldberg has donated her time to cook banquets for 100 people in need using whatever she finds at the local food bank, Good News Network reported on November 20, 2026. Far from spaghetti and canned sides, she makes restaurant-quality dishes like a lentil fritter spiced with caramelized onion, cinnamon and curry powder. Goldberg studied social work before a love of cooking competitions pulled her into the culinary arts, but fine dining’s food waste bothered her. “The main rule was, ‘Never run out of anything,’” she told TODAY. “So, we would just throw out so much food, it was insane.” She moved to private cheffing to make time to volunteer at Fort York Food Bank, and now has 180,000 Instagram followers. Anyone inspired doesn’t have to cook for 100, she says: ask your local food bank what it needs, because you might already have it at home.

title: A father-daughter business turns rhino dung into paper and gives villagers a reason to protect rhinos
summary: A father-daughter team in Assam, India, makes paper from rhino dung collected by locals, giving villagers who sometimes clash with rhinos a steady income and a reason to protect them, Good News Network reported on November 20, 2026. Elrhino Stationery co-founder Mahesh Chandra Bora, a retired mining engineer, got the idea after reading about rhino dung paper in Rajasthan and wondered why it couldn’t be done in Assam, home to some 2,900 greater one-horned rhinos. His first tests used his wife’s kitchen blender. His daughter Nisha left a 17-year corporate career to help, and Elrhino launched in 2014. Rhino and elephant dung harvested near reserves like Kaziranga and Pobitora national parks is washed and boiled to recover plant fibers, pulped, mixed with recycled paper or cotton waste, then pressed and dried into sheets. The range now includes notebooks, journals, paper bags, lampshades and playing cards.

title: Southern Screen Festival wraps its 16th year in Lafayette this weekend
summary: The 16th annual Southern Screen Festival runs November 19–22, 2026, in Lafayette, so this weekend is the final stretch, according to Downtown Lafayette’s listing and the festival’s own site. The four-day festival offers dozens of film screenings plus workshops, panels, parties and live performances, and promises to “entertain, educate, and inspire.” “Let Southern Screen show you how the heart of Cajun Country showcases emerging and innovative storytellers,” the listing says. The festival describes itself as packed with international screenings, industry panels, professional workshops, music and live performances, and says it is invested in building Acadiana’s cultural economy. Visitors driving downtown can use metered street parking, which Downtown Lafayette notes is free after 5 p.m. on weekdays and all day on weekends, or the Parc-Auto du Centre-Ville garage at 121 East Vermilion Street, which has 530 spaces.

title: Author Carrie Simon talks ‘The Girl Who Ate Flowers’ at CHB Lafayette this afternoon
summary: CHB Lafayette hosts a Q&A and book signing with author Carrie Simon on Saturday, November 21, 2026, at 3 p.m., according to Downtown Lafayette’s event listing. Simon will discuss her latest book, The Girl Who Ate Flowers, in a moderated conversation led by Rachel Comeaux Lanclos. The novel is set in the quiet town of Harvey, Louisiana, shattered by the disappearance and murder of twelve-year-old Susanne Lee; years later the case remains unsolved when an unrelenting investigative journalist from The Manhattan Times arrives determined to uncover the truth. RSVPs for the afternoon are handled through Bon Temps Tix, the listing says, and books will be available at the event. It’s a chance to hear a Louisiana-set mystery discussed by its author, then take home a signed copy.

title: Crafternoon brings free freestyle crafting for kids to the Main Library today
summary: The Lafayette Public Library’s Main Library hosts Crafternoon on Saturday, November 21, 2026, from 2 to 3 p.m. in the first-floor Craft Room, according to the library’s event calendar. “Come get crafty!” the listing says, promising freestyle crafting “with all supplies provided.” The program is aimed at ages 5 to 12, making it an easy, free Saturday-afternoon outing for families with school-age kids who want to make something with their hands. The same day, the library calendar also lists Makerspace Open Access at the Main Library, an every-third-Saturday session that lets patrons work independently on projects of their choosing, with self-guided tutorials for most applications and no registration required.

title: Santa visits the Main Library’s Story Castle on Tuesday
summary: Santa Claus is coming to the Lafayette Public Library’s Main Library on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, from 10 a.m. to noon in the first-floor Story Castle, according to the library’s event calendar. “Don’t miss Santa’s visit to the library!” the listing says. Children can take a picture with Santa using their parent’s own phone, then join a craft. The visit is open to ages 0 to 18, and families are welcome. It’s one of several Santa stops on the library’s calendar this Thanksgiving week; the calendar also lists a Santa visit at the North Regional Library that afternoon at 1 p.m. The Main Library’s Story Castle visit is in person, making it a holiday photo opportunity for families before the Thanksgiving break.
